headline: East Wall Porgies Stack Up While Blues Crash the Bunker and Bass Wait Their Turn
subhead: The bottom bite held steady all week on the New Haven and Milford rockpiles — bluefish are the loudest thing in the water right now, and the stripers are staging just behind them.
body_markdown:
The bottom bite never blinked this week, and that's the real story out of Central Connecticut Sound heading into the long weekend. Porgies and sea bass have been steady on every piece of structure from the New Haven breakwalls out to Falkner Island, and that consistency is buying time while the bigger story — the fall striper turnover — keeps loading up offstage.

Water temps are still soft for early September, running in the low-to-mid 70s on the western end and cooling off toward the high 60s as you push east toward New London. That gradient matters. It's kept bait schools from tightening into the kind of dense, panicked balls that trigger a real blitz. Bunker are thick in the harbor mouths and along the beaches from Stratford to Hammonasset, but they're still swimming loose and unbothered more often than not. Stripers are on them — captains working the Charles Island bar and the mouth of the Housatonic are marking fish under the pods on the graph — but they're eating opportunistically, not committing in numbers. We flagged this pattern last week: bait density needs to build further before the bass tip over into blitz mode, and with the moon building toward full on the 6th and 7th, the tidal push is about to get a lot stronger. That's usually the ingredient that's been missing. Give it seven to ten days.

Bluefish, meanwhile, have had zero patience for subtlety. They've been the most reliable thing happening in the zone, tearing through peanut bunker schools off the New Haven Harbor breakwalls, the Charles Island rip, and the reef structure off Hammonasset. That's exactly what we called for Labor Day week — warm water keeping them aggressive and spread out — and it's held. Metal is the move: half-ounce to one-ounce Kastmasters and Deadly Dicks worked fast through the froth, or bucktails with a strip of fresh bunker if you want to slow it down and pick off a bigger fish sitting under the chaos.

On the rockpiles, it's been a genuinely fun week for anyone who likes fishing light. The east wall at New Haven Harbor has been giving up porgies in the 10-to-12-inch class on the last two hours of the dropping tide, with high-low rigs baited on sandworms and green crab working best in 15 to 20 feet tight to the riprap. Sea bass are mixed right in with them, especially around the deeper pockets near the harbor entrance buoys — squid strips and Gulp swimming mullets on a bucktail teaser have been outproducing plain bait rigs when the current's got some push to it.

Falkner Island remains the money spot for anyone willing to make the run. The rockpiles on the north and west sides in 25 to 35 feet have been holding a mixed bag of porgies and sea bass all week, with the bigger sea bass — some pushing 3 pounds — coming on butterflied clam and squid combos fished on the bottom during the last of the incoming tide, when the current slackens enough to hold bottom without a half-pound of lead. Stratford Shoal is fishing similarly, though boat traffic has been heavier there with the holiday crowd, so early morning has been the difference between a full cooler and a picked-over pile.

Fluke are thinning out the way they always do this time of year, and that's not a surprise — this is the normal seasonal shuffle as the bigger fish slide out toward deeper structure ahead of the fall run, not a sign the bite's collapsed. There's still a window in the Milford Gulf and along the channel edges toward Charles Island, working white and chartreuse Gulp on 3/4-ounce bucktails on the last of the ebb. Numbers are down from August, but a few keeper-class fish are still coming off the deeper humps for anyone putting in the drift time.

Looking ahead, the wind pattern's been cooperative — nothing but light southwest breezes and clean water, which has kept the structure bite consistent and the harbor entrances fishable on both tides. That should hold through the weekend. The bigger question is what happens once the full moon tightens up the tidal flow. If the bunker schools along the Milford and Stratford beaches start bunching up the way they have in past Septembers, the first real blitz activity of the fall could break open right off the breakwalls — and that's a much better problem than the slow build we've had. Until then, the smart play is simple: fish the structure early and often for porgies and sea bass, keep a bucktail rigged for blues when the bunker get nervous, and keep an eye on Charles Island. That sandbar is usually the first place in this zone to tell you the fall bite has actually arrived.
